Berndt's Part I, Chapter 7, corollary to Entry 10: ∑_{k=1}^{n−1} φ_r(−k/n) = (n − n^{−r}) ζ(−r), where φ_r is analytically continued in r. The Lean does not construct φ. It takes it abstractly as the entire continuation of the series φ_r(x) = ∑((j+1)^r − (j+1+x)^r), Re r < 0, and these hypotheses determine φ uniquely on admissible x. The identity is stated as equality off a discrete set, with meromorphy of both sides. That is needed because Lean's ζ has a junk value at 1, which affects the right side at r = −1. These are implementation-level differences. The docstring cites only 'Chapter 7'; the module header names the Entry 10 corollary.

Source record 83a: the Wirsing constant is |λ₂| ≈ 0.3036630, the subdominant eigenvalue modulus of the GKW operator. Over holomorphic eigenfunctions on the Mayer disk, any eigenfunction with λ ≠ 0 extends past the boundary, so the nonzero eigenvalues are Mayer–Roepstorff's. The sup of |λ| over λ ≠ 1 is then |λ₂|. The only differences are the totalized sSup and the documented decision not to assert the spectral theorem.

The docstring says that at i = 0 'the product side has a zero factor while the series side does not vanish'. This is false. At i = 0 the terms for n and −n−1 have the same exponent (2k+1)n(n+1)/2 and opposite signs, so the absolutely convergent series sums to 0, matching the zero factor 1 − q^0 in the product. This also holds at q = 0, where the n = 0 and n = −1 terms give 1 − 1. The hypothesis 0 < i is harmless but not needed for the identity. The justification should be corrected or removed upstream. The proposed docstring drops it.

Andrews' JTP1 (Theory of Partitions, p. 22): ∑(−1)^n q^{(2k+1)n(n+1)/2 − in} = ∏_{n≥1}(1 − q^{(2k+1)n})(1 − q^{(2k+1)n−i})(1 − q^{(2k+1)(n−1)+i}). Shifting n to n+1 gives the Lean product exactly, and the identity follows from the Jacobi triple product with z = −q^{(2k+1)/2−i}. Lean adds 0 < i ≤ k. That restriction is standard in Andrews' use of the identity, but its documented rationale is wrong. I could not fetch the source TeX (no network).

This is Kimberling's theorem as given in Kärki–Lacroix–Rigo, JIS 13 (2010): the self-generating set from 1 under 2x and 4x−1 is 1,2,3,4,6,7,8,11,12,14,15,16,…, and with the first term dropped, its terms mod 2 give 0,1,0,0,1,0,1,0,0,1,0,…, the Fibonacci word. Checked by hand on the first terms. Truncated subtraction in 4x−1 never applies because every element is at least 1.

The text defines the same object: the number of distinct contiguous length-n factors of w, with the factor at i given by j ↦ w(i+j) and repeated occurrences collapsed. This matches ncard of the range of factor w n.

Durand–Leroy–Richomme define the complexity function p_w(n) of an infinite word over a finite alphabet as the number of distinct factors of length n. Lean matches this exactly. The finite alphabet guarantees the factor set is finite, so Set.ncard is never the junk value 0.

This matches Hausdorff's L^∞ moment criterion (Knill §115, third statement). This is the Hildebrandt–Schoenberg theorem: a sequence on ℕ^d is the moment sequence of a signed measure of bounded variation on [0,1]^d iff ∑_{k≤n} C(n,k)|Δ^{n−k}a_k| is bounded. diff a k n with k ≤ n equals the forward difference ∑ᵢ(−1)^i C(k,i) a_{n−k+i}, so the Lean sum is exactly that condition. Signed measures are encoded by their Jordan decomposition into finite measures on ℝ^d, integrated over the cube, which is equivalent to measures on the cube.

Then c = inf over paths of the max is a critical value with c ≥ ε. The module documents that it corrects Knill's slip of writing |b| > ε.

The Lean statement is trivially true. Take U = B(0,3) ∪ B(c,1) with c = (10,0,0), and let f be 1 where x₀ > 6 and 0 elsewhere. Then f is locally constant near every point of U, so HarmonicAt holds there (ContDiffAt 2 and Laplacian eventually 0). U contains the cube, f vanishes on the edges, and f(c) = 1 ≠ 0. Nothing requires U to be connected, or f to be nonzero on the component that contains the cube.

The article calls U a 'region', which conventionally means connected, but Lean has no connectedness. That word turns a trivial statement into Wavre's deep one, so the article states more than the Lean does.

Alon–Shikhelman, arXiv:1409.4192, define ex(n,T,H) as the maximum number of copies of T in an H-free graph on n vertices, for T and H without isolated vertices. The article never defines ω: it drops the hypotheses ω(x) = 1/x on [1,2] and x ω(x) = 1 + ∫_1^{x-1} ω for x ≥ 2, which pin down the Buchstab function on [1,∞). It also never says that the c_{n,i} are arbitrary reals or what kind of convergence the series has. The recursions themselves match Lean.

This is a documented correction of a misprint, not a weakening: the printed theorem has c_{n,i}/n where Lean has c_{n,i-1}/i. Differentiating x ω(x) in z gives i[(2n+3)c_{n+1,i} + c_{n+1,i-1}] = c_{n,i-1}, which is Lean's form. Integrating from z = -1 to 0 gives Lean's formula for c_{n+1,0}. c_{1,i} follows from 2/(3+z). The Lean statement is correct mathematics.

This is the type-A_n case of Panyushev's conjecture: the antichain size is homomesic under the Panyushev map (antichain rowmotion) with average rank/2. This is a documented strengthening of the classical (invertible) Rokhlin lemma, matching the cited Heinemann–Schmitt non-invertible version. Their preimage-tower form implies this forward-image form: with C, T⁻¹C, …, T^{-(n-1)}C disjoint, take B = T^{-(n-1)}C. Then each T^k B lies in the disjoint measurable set T^{-(n-1-k)}C and has outer measure ≥ μ(C), so the union has outer measure ≥ nμ(C) > 1−ε. StandardBorelSpace is needed, as the module doc explains. 'Realizable' is never defined, and the Lean notion is not the standard one. Lean asks that the fixed-point set of T^{n+1} has |u_n| elements (natAbs), so it only constrains absolute values: sign-alternating sequences such as (−1)^n L_n count as realizable. The index is also shifted (u_n counts points of period n+1). A reader would assume u_n = Per_n(T) ≥ 0.

Hadwiger's theorem: the continuous, rigid-motion-invariant valuations on nonempty compact convex sets in ℝⁿ form a vector space of dimension n+1, spanned by the intrinsic volumes. Farley (2022) answers Björner's question: every geometric lattice of finite rank, of any cardinality, has an injection from atoms to coatoms with a ≤ f(a). For a spanning P ⊆ ℝ^d (d ≥ 1), the lattice of affine flats spanned by subsets of P has rank d+1 ≥ 2. Its atoms are the points of P and its coatoms correspond bijectively to the affine hyperplanes spanned by subsets of P, so Lean's statement follows. The translation from lattices to geometry is the only difference.

HasTangentLineAt is an unoriented tangent-line condition (the secant is close to the line ℝv, either direction). A closed curve with a cusp meets it at the cusp, but has no differentiable parametrization with p' ≠ 0 there: both branches leave the cusp in the same direction, while p(t0+h) − p(t0) ≈ h·p'(t0) leaves in opposite directions for h > 0 and h < 0. So ¬Claim follows from an elementary example and does not capture Ward's 1937 theorem, which concerns Fréchet's (oriented) tangent. The root cause is in HasTangentLineAt / ScottishBookProblem117Claim; see those nodes.

Rosser's theorem says that every consistent, effectively axiomatized theory with enough arithmetic has an undecidable sentence. The Lean statement assumes the arithmetization: representability, the diagonal lemma and the negative representability principle are all hypotheses. It also adds a truth predicate so that it can conclude the sentence is true. The docstring documents this abstraction, so it is reported, not fixed. 'Regular (Radon)' is loose. Lean asks for `IsFiniteMeasure μ` together with Mathlib's `Regular μ`, which means finite on compact sets, outer regular, and inner regular on open sets by compact sets.

Folland's Lusin theorem (Thm 7.10) works with an LCH space, a Radon measure, and a complex-valued f that vanishes outside a set of finite measure. Hercher's Main Theorem says there are no m-cycles with m ≤ 91 for the shortcut Collatz map, where an m-cycle has m local minima (equivalently m odd runs). The docstring's claim '(x ∣ y)_w = Metric.gromovProduct x y w (basepoint third, as in Mathlib)' is false. Mathlib's docstring and gromovProduct_eq put the basepoint first. So the Lean is not Gromov's four-point condition (Gromov 1987, §1.1, cited in the module docstring). Example: in ℝ take w = R, x = z = 0, y = 2R. Then gromovProduct x y w = R, gromovProduct y z w = R and gromovProduct x z w = 0, which forces δ ≥ R. So ℝ, a 0-hyperbolic ℝ-tree, is not δ-hyperbolic for any δ. More generally, taking x = z and w a midpoint of x and y shows that any space with midpoints has diameter ≤ 2δ. For geodesic spaces the Lean notion is therefore just boundedness.

Lean doesn't match the source (needs-lean-change). In Kabluchko–Marynych–Sulzbach the coefficients of the expansion are explicit polynomials in x (with H_0 = 1), and that is where the theorem's content lies. Here H : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ → ℝ is existentially quantified with no constraint. For fixed θ, the map (n,k) ↦ x with n ≥ 2 is injective except for θ in a countable set, because a collision between two pairs fixes θ uniquely. So for those θ one can take H_0 to be the exact ratio of the PMF to the Gaussian factor and H_j = 0 for j ≥ 1, which makes the difference zero. That makes the statement nearly vacuous; for a singleton L = {θ} with generic θ it is trivial. The docstring mentions that H is 'existentially bound' but doesn't flag how much this weakens the theorem. Upstream fix: specify the coefficient polynomials, or at least require H j · θ to be polynomial with H 0 = 1.

Minor: the source takes the supremum over all integers k, while the Lean takes only 1 ≤ k ≤ n. Outside the support the PMF is 0 but the Gaussian term isn't, so the Lean statement is slightly weaker there too.

Wikipedia's spherical law of cosines is cos c = cos a cos b + sin a sin b cos C for a spherical triangle on the unit sphere. Lean encodes the triangle with coordinates in ℝ^3 and gives the angle at w through its cosine. The quotient is the cosine of the angle between the tangent vectors u − (u·w)w and v − (v·w)w, because their dot product simplifies to u·v − (u·w)(v·w). With C in (0, π), this fixes C. These are implementation-level differences only. The hypotheses on c and C are unused, and the docstring documents this.

The article only says 'The defining four-point inequality of a δ-hyperbolic space.' and never states the inequality, its quantifiers or the hypothesis.

Gromov's four-point inequality is (x|z)_w ≥ min((x|y)_w,(y|z)_w) − δ with all products based at w. Mathlib's Metric.gromovProduct takes the basepoint first (gromovProduct x y z = (d(x,y)+d(x,z)−d(y,z))/2, 'Gromov product of y and z with respect to x'). So the Lean inequality is min((y|w)_x,(z|w)_y) − δ ≤ (z|w)_x, which mixes basepoints. Counterexample: an equilateral triangle with side 2L (genuinely 0-hyperbolic) violates it for δ < L when x = z. This inherits the mismatch in Metric.IsDeltaHyperbolic.

The title 'Four point' is humanized from the Lean name (lint title-from-lean-name) and is not how a mathematician names the result, e.g. 'Four-point inequality for δ-hyperbolic spaces'. δ is in backticks instead of TeX.

It rejects genuinely 0-hyperbolic spaces: an equilateral 3-point space with side 2L needs δ ≥ L (take x = z), and ℝ is not δ-hyperbolic for any δ (take x = −a, y = a, w = 0, which forces δ ≥ a). Trees likewise fail. So IsGromovHyperbolic also does not capture Gromov hyperbolicity.

Rojas (2015) answers Auerbach's Scottish Book Problem 148: for nonzero P, the complement of the zero set is connected iff every irreducible real factor is sign-semidefinite. The Lean condition is an unoriented tangent line, and a cusp satisfies it: γ(s) = (s², s³, 0) at s = 0 with v = e₁ gives ‖(0, s³, 0)‖ ≤ ε s² for small s. No parametrization of it can have p'(t₀) ≠ 0 at the cusp, because secants from the two sides would have to point in opposite directions. Nat.nth returns 0 past the end of a finite set. If some p_s = 2, then Π^0 = {primes ρ ≢ 1 mod every p_s} = {2}, so r_{i,0} = 0 for i ≥ 1. The composition k_0 = ω(x^n − 1), other k_j = 0, then makes every block product 0 once ω ≥ 2, and each bound reads 1 ≤ x^{…}. Likewise Π^j is empty for j ≥ 1 when 2 is ordered after p_j ('in any order'). In the source, products past the end of Π^j are undefined, so those compositions are not admissible. For every even n the Lean statement is therefore nearly vacuous, a material weakening of Theorem 1. The documented change k_j ∈ ℕ instead of ℤ⁺ is justified (the n = 3, x = 2 counterexample checks out).

The article quotes the source's min–max formula and says it is 'stated equivalently … as the existence of a composition k meeting every bound'. It never writes out the inequality Lean states (1 + ∏_{j≤t} ∏_{i<k_j} r_{i,j} ≤ x^{∏_{s≤t} p_s^{a_s}} for all t ≤ m). It omits the hypothesis a_i > 0 and the zero value of r_{i,j} past the end of a finite Π^j.

Both formalize the same theorem of Smith for different definitions of the constant, so the titles have to be distinct within NumberTheory. This one is built on the 'Schur–Siegel–Smyth trace constant' article, so it can take the name that article uses.

Smith (Annals 2024, Theorem 1.1) finds infinitely many totally positive algebraic integers with absolute trace below about 1.898304. If ρ were admissible with ρ > 1.898304, the finite exceptional set would contain infinitely many elements, so C86 ≤ 1.898304 < 1.89831. Reznick's definition calls a lattice parallelogram clean when its only boundary lattice points are its vertices, and the Lean matches it. Katz–Lindell (2nd ed.) Theorem 12.16 is asymptotic: if f is one-way, then Lamport's scheme is one-time secure. The Lean is the exact finite bound from its proof, Pr[I inverts] ≥ ε/(2ℓ), for a fixed f on a finite set. The inverter matches KL's: plant y at a uniform (i*, b*), abort when m_{i*} = b*, output σ'_{i*} when m'_{i*} = b*. The docstring calls this 'the reduction behind' the theorem, which is accurate. The only difference is concrete versus asymptotic.

Gaetz–Gao (arXiv:1811.05501, PAMS 148, 2020) prove that the weak order on S_n is strongly Sperner, hence Sperner.
